A11y note on blurring, in general, and on combination of blurring and motion:
The minimal and relatively slow-moving animation is an inclusive approach for the motion. Maybe, the blur could be tweaked a bit to avoid a response from users with newly acquired sensitivity (i.e. using a Kit tail instead of a glare)? In general, some users (including those who do not identify as having a disability) have been reporting that blurred backgrounds are making them feel dizzy. 

Recent usability research data, shows a growing number of users reporting fast motion and blurring as being nauseating or triggering migraines - those users who report starting experiencing it in the last few years are mostly non-disabled users. CX Insights (Tritus Technologies) had a larger study done that included deeper conversations with users who reported newly acquired sensitivity. Some of these user mentioned their new discomfort from fast-moving visuals. And most of users with more severe reactions (incl. vomiting during following a Figma mockup review on a larger screen that has been a part of their routine work) have had (or suspected they had) COVID before they had this sensitivity onset. Most of them have never been diagnosed with any Long COVID or related complications. 

Sadly, I cannot link to a report above because this was presented on a workshop led by the CX Insights and the research was paid by their commercial customer. But there are 3 available peer-reviewed papers that research similar hypothesis:
* Frontiers cohort paper (2023) reports vestibular symptoms were commonly mentioned and tracks dizziness over follow-up in post-COVID participants. 
* Earlier Frontiers paper (2022) investigates persistent vestibular damage in people with vertigo after COVID-19. Pendulum test showed 1 in 3 participants had concerns while visually tracking a moving object.
* Springer paper (2025) reports that "dizziness, vertigo, and balance problems are among the most frequently reported neurological complaints following COVID-19 infection", while reporting 1 in 4 participants "reported that their dizziness worsened with stress, while 30.7% stated that it increased with movement".

Numbers-wise, in the US, NHANES 2001–2004) found 35.4% of US adults 40+ had vestibular dysfunction (often correlated with dizziness/balance issues). CDC estimates that by the end of 2022, 77.5% of Americans had had COVID-19 at least once and 6.9-8% of adults in the US have had Long COVID. So, in the US alone, there could be as much as 3 in 4 adults who may have increased discomfort and 1 in 14 is risking to have a more severe reaction].

Importantly, none of these users reported using "Prefers reduced motion" settings and vast majority of them were not aware this feature exists in modern OSes. Thus, relying on this OS-level preference alone is not sufficient.

Is it possible to move the sub-menu indication (">" chevron) to the left side of the label or closer to the text label, i.e. at the end of the on-screen string?

This is an existing issue that we could try to resolve with the redesign: ATM many labels of controls on a panel are too far removed from the indicators that these controls are going to open a sub-menu (their chevrons).

Enhancement for default themes and recommendation for Contrast themes (HCM on Windows and Increased Contrast on Linux and Mac):
Could we increase a color contrast of the border of the menu itself against the menu's own background? Right now it's 1.6:1 and while it is clearly distinguishable against the blue and greens of the example site below it, we probably want to make sure that any website below the menu would be clearly separated from the menu by Firefox. 

Having a sufficient color contrast between the menu border color and menu background color would be highly beneficial for this important separation of chrome vs webcontent, because dark websites would get light menu background to be in contrast with the webcontent, and the light/white backgrounded websites would get that visible border that would help users to discern the menu panel against the website below it.

Making the border of the panel darker is highly recommended: at least 3:1 or higher in color contrast against the menu background, but probably 4.5:1 and more would give more reliable visual separation for users with low vision, with color deficiency, and even users with glare on their screens too!

The "pressed"/"expanded" state for the menu has very subtle visual change that may make some users to not know if the menu is, in fact, visible and if the block below it is, in fact, that menu item called.

While this may not affect the experience with the large menu like this in an extreme way, there are cases, like a shield panel, when a smaller panel is opened and then a user could navigate to the subview of this panel - in this case some users with cognitive disabilities may loose the connection between the subview and the menu button. 

Having clear "pressed" state would help users to reinforce that this menu button is, in fact, still pressed and the panel they see comes from Firefox (and could be dismissed by clicking to this pressed menu button again). ATM the only change of the pressed vs default state is in background color - and this change is only 1.3:1 in color contrast (of the lighter purple against the lightest purple toolbar background). 

The color contrast should be at least 3:1 OR it should rely to something else beyond color alone. For instance, adding a border to the pressed button (with the same color that the foreground of the button is using) would resolve this issue and provide a clear state change indication that does not rely on color alone. In the current scenario, the darker purple of the button foreground color against lightest purple from the toolbar background would give amazing 5.8:1 in luminosity ratio (color contrast).

 It would also help users of custom themes where the developers of the theme may miss the color readability as well.

Issue:
While this lighter purple (#945af2 per the Colour Contrast Analyser's eye dropper) is acceptable to be used for graphics, including essential graphics like image buttons, the text however ("Firefox is ready to update" in this case) does fail the WCAG 2.x minimum color contrast requirements against even the darker part of this gradient - it should have color contrast for the text (white ATM) against the background (gradient purple to orange) of at the very least 4.5:1 (Level AA), but we hope to ensure text has 7:1 or more in color contrast (for the Level AAA compliance and ease of readability). 

Currently, the light purple against white text gives 4.2:1 in contrast ratio (failing 4.5 benchmark) deteriorating even further by the end of the string to 3.4:1, for longer strings this could go as low as 2.7:1 (not sufficient even for informative graphics and states differentiation). 

This has to be resolved because it is very visible WCAG failure and it affects the readability of the string that the team so thoughtfully crafted to add in the banner. 4.5:1 in color contrast should be the bare minimum for all parts of text against this gradient background. For instance, black color would satisfy this requirement from the purple (5:1) to the orange (7.8:1) sections.

Enhancement: Would that be possible to remove the gradual transparency for high contrast modes (when `forced-colors` on Windows and/or `prefers-contrast` on Linux and MacOS are active)? This could be a helpful affordance and help users who need higher clarify of the interface to distinguish tabs easier as well

It's not clear what this button is symbolizing, i.e. if it's a user-selected icon (which it is probably not, given that the user profile picture appears on the top left side, next to the menu button) or an extension logo, then this would not need to be adjusted for discernibility (this is not in the browser's control).

But it seems that this may be some Firefox own tool - then we would need to make sure its border (light gray now) has at least 3:1 in color contrast against the toolbar background, then we could keep the inner image in any other way. ATM the light gray border against the white toolbar background gives only 1.6:1 in color contrast, which is below WCAG 2.1/2.2 Non-text Color Contrast guidelines of 3:1 or more, and it is hard to distinguish this logo control on the toolbar

could the color of this disabled control be made a bit darker? It's currently 1.6:1 and would be easy to miss. While disabled states are technically excluded from WCAG compliance, internally we are aiming to still make sure the disabled controls are somewhat discernible - after all, these controls remain on-screen in their disabled state to indicate that, in some other situation, this control could become enabled. 

 For instance, the [disabled control color token in Acorn DS](https://acorn.firefox.com/latest/desktop/design-tokens/color-pCFFM8pk#section-color-ca) provides 2.7:1 in color contrast against white background - this makes disabled controls a bit more discernible. 

The goal is to get as close to 3:1 with the disabled foreground color against its background as possible (the lighter purple vs white, in this case), while maintaining at least 3:1 in color contrast between two states' foreground colors (the dark purple for enabled control vs lighter purple for disabled control, in this case).
